To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the M‐channel is inhibited by the depletion of membrane PIP2 following Gq/phosholipase‐C catalysed PIP₂ hydrolysis, that this inhibition is mediated by a direct action of the product, IP₃, on the M‐channel, and that these effects are modulated by the rate of PIP₂ resynthesis.
the M‐channel is regulated by the products of PIP₂ hydrolysis, in addition to PIP₂ depletion.

the effects of receptor stimulation on M(Kv7) channels are determined by the relative rates of PIP2 synthesis and PIP2 hydrolysation, and that these effects can be mediated either by PIP2 reduction or by products of PIP₂ hydrolysis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms of M‐channel modulation in neurons and how these are affected by changes in membrane PIP₂ levels.

the molecular basis of the inhibition of neuronal M‐currents by muscarinic and other Gq/11 receptor agonists, which is a fundamental process in the regulation of neuronal excitability and synaptic plasticity.
understanding how the activity of M‐channels is regulated in different cell types and how this regulation is altered in disease states such as epilepsy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
M‐current inhibition in sympathetic neurons is primarily PIP2‐dependent, but that the PIP2 depletion is not the sole mechanism of inhibition.
PIP2 hydrolysation products can modulate the activity of M‐channels, but that this can occur via different mechanisms depending on the cell and the stimulus used.

the inhibition of M‐channels by receptor stimulation can be achieved through depletion of PIP2 or through release of Ca2+ and activation of Ca2+‐sensitive K+ channels, depending on neuronal type and receptor subtype.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
M‐channel inhibition in sympathetic neurons is primarily substrate‐dependent (depleting PIP2), but can be product‐dependent (releasing Ca2+) if PIP2 synthesis is blocked.

M‐current inhibition is primarily a PIP2 depletion phenomenon, but that the depletion may be achieved through different mechanisms, and that the mechanism is dependent on Ca2+ levels and PIP2 turnover rates.
the effects of Gq/11 receptor stimulation on M‐current inhibition can be divided into two phases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
M(Kv7) channels are regulated by PIP2 levels in the membrane, and that this regulation is altered by products of PIP hydrolysis.
the effects of receptor activation on M‐channels are highly context dependent and cannot be generalized.
the regulation of M‐channels by PIP2, PIP2 hydrolysate products, or both, depends on cell type and on the availability of Ca2+ and PIP2.
